(p-214)Surah al-Falaq

Makki, though this is disputed, and its verses are five.

﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak.﴾ "Al-falaq" means the dawn (al-subh), like al-faraq; because the night is split (yuflaqu) and separated (yufraqu) from it. It is on the pattern fa'al in the sense of maf'ul (object), since each of the split thing and that from which it is split is split. It has also been said that it is what has split away from its column (of light). It has also been said that it is everything that Allah the Exalted splits: the earth for plants, the mountains for springs, the clouds for rains, the grain and the date-stone for what comes out of them, and other things. In linking seeking refuge to the name of the Lord, joined to al-falaq, which indicates light after darkness, expansion after constriction, and opening after closure, there is a gracious promise of returning the one seeking refuge from what he seeks refuge from and delivering him from it, and a strengthening of his hope by reminding him of some similar instances, and a further encouragement to him to be earnest and attentive in knocking at the door of seeking refuge with Him, the Exalted. As for the indication that whoever is able to remove the darkness of the night from this world is able to remove from the one seeking refuge what he fears, as it has been said, "so no", since the one seeking refuge has no doubt about His, the Exalted's, power over that, so as to need to be alerted to it.

﴿From the evil of what He has created﴾. That is: from the evil of what He created, of the two weighty ones (al-thaqalayn, humankind and jinn) and others, whatever it may be, of beings that have natures and volition. As you see, this includes all evils. Whoever imagines that seeking refuge here is from bodily harms, and that it covers humans and others only in respect of what is the object of seeking refuge, and then makes this generality the basis for attributing the Lord to the daybreak (al-falaq), has strayed far from the truth. The attribution of evil to Him is because of His being specific to the world of creation (ʿalam al-khalq), which is founded on the mixing of differing substances and the interaction of their opposing qualities, which entails coming into being and corruption. As for the world of command (ʿalam al-amr), it is pure good, entirely free of any admixture of evil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And from the evil of darkness when it gathers﴾ is a specification of some evils by mention, although they are included in what precedes it, because the need to seek refuge from it is more pressing, due to how frequently it occurs. Also, naming the thing sought refuge from shows more clearly the concern for seeking refuge, and is more likely to bring about protection. That is: and from the evil of a night whose darkness is thick, drawn from His saying: ﴿to the darkness of the night﴾. The root meaning of al-ghasaq is the flowing of tears. The attribution of evil to the night is because evil is associated with it through its occurrence in it. It is also because evil does not encompass all of its individual instances or all of its parts. It is restricted by His saying: ﴿when it gathers﴾, meaning its darkness has entered into everything, because its occurrence is more frequent in it, and guarding oneself against it is more difficult and arduous. For this reason it was said: "The night is more concealing for mischief."

It was also said: al-Ghasiq is the moon when it is full, and its gathering (wuqub) is its entering into eclipse and becoming dark. This is based on what has been narrated: "From 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took my hand, pointed to the moon, and said: Seek refuge in Allah, Exalted is He, from the evil of this ghasiq when it gathers."

It was also said: the reference to the moon as al-ghasiq is because its body is dark, and it only shines by the light of the sun. Its gathering is the mihaq (the dark phase) at the end of the month. The astrologers consider it an ill omen, and for this reason sorcerers do not practice the kind of magic that causes illness except at that time. It was said: this is the most appropriate interpretation in light of the occasion of revelation.

It was also said: al-Ghasiq is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), and its gathering is its setting, because when it sets, diseases and plagues become widespread.

It was also said: it is every evil that befalls a person, and its gathering is its onset.

﴿And from the evil of those who blow upon knots﴾. That is: and from the evil of souls, or of the female sorceresses who tie knots in threads and blow upon them. *Al-nafth* (blowing with a little saliva) is blowing with spittle, and it is said: without saliva. It is also read *al-nafithat* and *al-nafathat* without an alif. Its definiteness (*al-* in *al-nafthat*) is either for specific reference (*al-ahd*) or to signify that the evil encompasses all of them and is purely theirs. Its specific mention is because of what Ibn 'Abbas and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them both, related: there was a Jewish boy who served the Prophet ﷺ, and he had some of the Prophet's ﷺ comb teeth with him. He gave them to the Jews, and they practised sorcery against him, peace be upon him, through them. Labid ibn al-A'sam, a Jew, and his daughters took charge of this, and they are "those who blow upon knots." He buried them in the well of Aris, and the Prophet ﷺ fell ill. Then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended with the two *mu'awwidhatayn* (the two protective surahs) and informed him of the location of the sorcery, of who had worked it, and with what. The Prophet ﷺ then sent 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and al-Zubayr and 'Ammar, may Allah be pleased with them both. They drained the water of the well until it looked like the soaking of henna. Then they lifted the *ra'uthah* of the well, which is the rock placed at the bottom of the well, and from beneath it they brought out the teeth, along with a cord in which eleven knots had been tied, pierced with a needle. They brought them to the Prophet ﷺ, and he began to recite the two *mu'awwidhatayn* over them. Each time he recited a verse, a knot came undone, and he ﷺ felt relief until the last knot was released from him upon the completion of the two surahs. He ﷺ then rose as if he had been freed from a fetter. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall we not kill the wicked one?" He ﷺ said: "As for me, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has granted me well-being, and I dislike stirring up evil among the people."

'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "The Prophet ﷺ never became angry with a rage that sought revenge for himself, except when the matter was for Allah, the Exalted; then he became angry for Allah's sake and took revenge."

It has also been said: the intended meaning of blowing upon knots is the nullification of men's resolves through stratagems, and it is a metaphor drawn from softening a knot by blowing saliva upon it so that it may be easily undone.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And from the evil of an envier when he envies﴾. That is: when he manifests what is in his soul of envy and acts upon its requirement, by arranging the preliminaries of evil and the beginnings of harm to the envied person, whether by word or by deed. The restriction to this condition is because the harm of envy falls upon the envier himself before anyone else, and not upon anyone other than him.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the two Mu'awwidhatayn (the two protective surahs) is as if he had recited the Books that Allah the Exalted has sent down."
